statement: The graph shows how far Zara was from home during a bike ride. How many kilometres did she ride altogether?

figure.alt: A line graph of distance from home in kilometres against time in hours, from 0 to 6 hours. The line rises from 0 km to 12 km in the first hour, stays flat at 12 km until hour 2, rises to 20 km at hour 3, stays flat at 20 km until hour 4, then falls steadily to 0 km at hour 6.

choices.misconception: I gave the length of the whole ride in hours instead of the distance.
I read only the first part of the ride, up to the first flat stretch.
I read the highest point on the graph, which is only the ride out, not the ride back.
I added the heights of the two flat stretches, 12 and 20.

hints: What does a flat part of this graph mean?
The graph shows distance from home, not distance ridden. Rising means riding away, falling means riding back, and flat means standing still. Add up every stretch she rode.
She rode 12 km out, then 8 km further out to reach 20 km, then 20 km back home.

solutions.reliable: Read each piece. Hour 0 to 1: from 0 to 12 km, so 12 km ridden. Hour 1 to 2: flat, so she stopped. Hour 2 to 3: from 12 to 20 km, so 8 km more. Hour 3 to 4: flat, stopped again. Hour 4 to 6: from 20 km back to 0, so 20 km. Total 12 + 8 + 20 = 40 km. The transferable idea: on a distance-from-home graph, add every rise and every fall, and treat flat parts as rests.
solutions.elegant: She finished where she started, so she rode back exactly as far as she rode out. The furthest point is 20 km, so the ride was 20 + 20 = 40 km.

whyOnTest: Graph questions check that you know what the vertical axis measures: distance from home is not the same as distance travelled.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
